details.title: TwinTrace: Counterfactual Mutation Localization in Speech
details.description:
Overview Every example is a pair of causal twins. The left and right channels begin from the exact same three-second mixture of two real human readers and then pass through two four-stage audio-production histories. The histories are identical except for exactly one hidden mutation. Your job is to localize that mutation and explain what changed. This setup models a practical media-forensics and pipeline-regression problem: two rendered assets sound related, the processing log is unavailable or untrusted, and an engineer must identify the one configuration edit that caused them to diverge. Because speech content, crop, speaker mixture, and unaffected stages are shared within a pair, the model must compare acoustic evidence across channels instead of recognizing a phrase or speaker. There are three mutation types: level_change: one operation stays at the same stage position but changes between mild, moderate, and strong. replace: one stage is replaced by a different operation. swap: two adjacent stages exchange order. Each history uses four distinct operations selected from: bandlimit: removes low and high frequency content. room_echo: adds delayed room-like reflections. colored_noise: adds spectrally colored background noise. compressor: applies nonlinear dynamic-range compression. hard_clip: applies saturation-like amplitude clipping. resample: applies a lower-rate conversion and restoration. quantize: applies reduced-precision companding and reconstruction. Every stage is represented as operation@level, where level is mild, moderate, or strong. Effect parameters vary continuously inside each level and independently of readers and spoken content. Later shared stages may attenuate or reshape the mutation's trace, so success requires comparative spectro-temporal reasoning. Task Specification Train or fine-tune an audio model using the labeled pairs in train.csv. For every row in test.csv, submit one mutation_json object with exactly four fields: edit: one of level_change, replace, or swap. position: the one-based location of the mutation. For a swap, this is the first of the two exchanged positions. before: the affected stage token from the left-channel history, or the two affected tokens for a swap. after: the affected stage token from the right-channel history, or the reversed two-token sequence for a swap. The public training set has 1,801 pairs from 32 reader groups. The hidden test has 502 pairs from eight disjoint reader groups, so solutions must transfer to unseen voices and passages. Each released file is a stereo PCM-16 WAV with exactly three seconds per channel at 16 kHz. Channel 1 is the before render and channel 2 is the after render. Dataset The public dataset contains: train.csv: labeled training rows. test.csv: test rows whose mutations are hidden. sample_submission.csv: a valid training-prior submission template. train/audio/: paired training WAV files. test/audio/: paired test WAV files. Audio paths are relative to the public dataset root. train.csv Columns id (string): opaque row identifier. audio_path (string): relative path to one stereo WAV pair. mutation_json (JSON string): the single mutation connecting the left and right histories. test.csv Columns id (string): opaque row identifier. audio_path (string): relative path to one stereo WAV pair. The public files do not expose source filenames, readers, chapters, transcripts, crop offsets, operation parameters, random states, or split-family identifiers. Opaque ids and fixed media properties are non-semantic. Submission Format Submit exactly one row for every test id. Columns must appear exactly in the order id,mutation_json. mutation_json must be a JSON object no longer than 320 characters with exactly the keys edit, position, before, and after. Do not add probabilities, explanations, or extra keys. Stage tokens must use a published operation, one @ separator, and a published level. For level_change, before and after are one-element arrays containing the same operation at different levels. For replace, they are one-element arrays containing different operations. For swap, they are two-element arrays, after must be the reverse of before, and position must be 1, 2, or 3. Example header: id,mutation_json Example row: cta_0042eee2aff31fd1,"{""edit"":""level_change"",""position"":3,""before"":[""compressor@mild""],""after"":[""compressor@strong""]}" Example row: cta_005ae1ec341f905c,"{""edit"":""swap"",""position"":2,""before"":[""room_echo@moderate"",""hard_clip@mild""],""after"":[""hard_clip@mild"",""room_echo@moderate""]}" These ids and payloads illustrate format only and are not hidden answers. Evaluation The TwinTrace Mutation Score gives exact-match credit while preserving interpretable partial credit for the four required decisions. For every structurally valid row: Exact is 1 only when edit type, position, before, and after all match; otherwise 0. Edit is 1 when the mutation type matches; otherwise 0. Position is 1 when the one-based location matches; otherwise 0. Before is 1 when the affected left-channel token sequence matches exactly; otherwise 0. After is 1 when the affected right-channel token sequence matches exactly; otherwise 0. RowScore = 0.30 × Exact + 0.20 × Edit + 0.20 × Position + 0.15 × Before + 0.15 × After. The final score is the mean RowScore across all 502 hidden rows. Higher is better. The theoretical minimum is 0.0, the theoretical maximum is 1.0, and a perfect submission scores exactly 1.0. Missing, extra, duplicated, or foreign ids; missing, extra, or reordered columns; and an empty submission raise InvalidSubmissionError. A row-local fault—including malformed or oversized JSON, missing or extra JSON keys, a non-integer or out-of-range position, an unknown edit, operation, or level, or a mutation whose fields contradict its edit semantics—scores 0 for that row without crashing or leaking private data. The sample training-prior submission scores 0.1412. A deterministic training-only CPU baseline using paired waveform and spectral statistics scores 0.2521, leaving 74.8% absolute headroom to perfect. Intended Approach Strong solutions should use a two-tower or Siamese audio encoder with shared weights, channel-to-channel cross-attention, or learned difference features over log-mel spectrograms or waveforms. Suitable backbones include audio spectrogram transformers, wav2vec2/HuBERT-style encoders, modern audio foundation encoders, and temporal CNNs. Multi-head outputs can predict edit type, position, operation identity, and treatment level, followed by a constrained decoder that enforces the published mutation grammar. Independent single-channel tagging is insufficient because the answer is defined by the contrast between the two renders. Useful evidence includes frequency-response differences, echo-tail changes, residual-noise color, nonlinear distortion, quantization artifacts, and the way a local edit propagates through later shared stages. Originality and Practical Value This is a paired counterfactual change-localization benchmark, not a request to recover either complete hidden production history. Every label identifies the minimal edit connecting two matched renders, including its exact location and calibrated before/after states. The same abstraction applies to detecting accidental changes in audio mastering, streaming transcodes, archival restoration, and reproducible media builds when pipeline logs are missing. The synchronized twin design removes content and speaker differences within each row while the disjoint-reader test split prevents memorizing voices across train and test. The benchmark therefore measures learned comparative audio reasoning under controlled interventions. Runtime and Dependencies Solutions run in the offline Eris environment on one A10G GPU. Use only dependencies, model weights, and other artifacts available inside the environment or packaged with the submission. Network access and hosted inference or recognition services are not allowed. The challenge-specific model must be trained or fine-tuned on the supplied public training data and must create one submission.csv following the exact schema within the platform runtime limit. What Not To Use Submissions may be rejected before payout if they use direct public-source lookup, recovered original filenames or identities, transcript search, exact or robust fingerprint matching against external speech archives, id/hash/row-order/file-size shortcuts, generator or random-state reversal, manual hidden-test labeling, hosted commercial audio-recognition APIs, hardcoded answer maps, grader/filesystem exploitation, or a fixed rule-only pipeline that does not learn from the supplied training pairs. Open pretrained audio models are allowed when their weights and inference run locally; the challenge-specific comparison model must be trained or fine-tuned on the provided public data.

details.title: Serial Crystallography Lattice Indexing
details.description:
Serial Crystallography Lattice Indexing Overview Recover a physically equivalent reciprocal-lattice basis, estimate the detector-position correction, and assign Miller indices to requested Bragg peaks in anonymized single-shot serial-crystallography packets. Each packet is derived from one real diffraction event and contains 12–18 target-lattice peaks plus 4–6 deterministically generated secondary-lattice distractors. Spot order is shuffled, and requested probe HKLs always belong to the target lattice. The stored basis is not unique. The evaluator accepts all 48 signed axis permutations, but one operator must explain both the submitted basis and probe HKLs. All fitting, validation, and calibration must use only the released public data. Solutions have 10 CPU cores, 62.5 GiB RAM, and 90 minutes; no GPU or runtime network is required. Intended approach Estimate reciprocal-cell scale and HKL ranges from the labeled training packets. Use pairwise-vector voting, coefficient search, RANSAC, FFT-style voting, or another robust consensus method to separate the majority target lattice from the secondary orientation and propose bases. Assign integer HKLs by constrained rounding or local search, score basis/HKL consistency under crystallographic equivalence, and calibrate indexability on train-only validation. Submission-first workflow Treat sample_submission.csv as a format example, not a solution. Produce and validate a complete test prediction from your first train-validated method before extended tuning. Whenever a later method improves held-out training performance, immediately checkpoint a fresh complete ./working/submission.csv; do not leave a stronger method only in an exploratory training script. What not to use Do not retrieve, fingerprint, or run CrystFEL/DIALS against public source streams to recover event identity or answers. Do not use source filenames, event tags, raw row order, archive offsets, file metadata, public IDs, packet paths, or information outside public/. Do not read private answers or grader/platform internals. Do not use hosted or closed-source APIs. Do not exploit malformed JSON, duplicate IDs, foreign spot IDs, parser behavior, or hard-coded hidden answers. Evaluation Submit id,prediction_json in exactly that order. Each JSON object contains a finite 3×3 reciprocal_basis, a finite two-value det_shift_mm, indexability in [0,1], and exactly one integer (h,k,l) entry for every requested local spot_id in probe_hkl. For each of the 48 signed/permuted operators op: basis_rms = RMS(predicted_basis - op @ true_basis) basis_score(op) = exp(-((basis_rms / 0.012)^2)) hkl_score(op) = fraction of requested probe HKLs correct under the same op joint(op) = 0.45basis_score(op) + 0.35hkl_score(op) The evaluator selects the operator with maximum joint(op) and keeps its basis and HKL components. Detector shift and confidence are then scored as: shift_score = exp(-((||predicted_shift - true_shift|| / 0.040)^2)) lattice_quality = (0.45basis_score + 0.35hkl_score) / 0.80 calibration = lattice_quality * clip(1 - |indexability - lattice_quality|, 0, 1) row_score = 0.45basis_score + 0.35hkl_score 0.15shift_score + 0.05calibration final_score = mean(row_score) Higher is better. Scores range from 0.0 to 1.0, and a perfect physically equivalent prediction scores exactly 1.0. For a perfect basis and HKL prediction, lattice_quality = 1; submitting indexability = 1 makes calibration = 1 simultaneously, so the four row-score terms total 0.45 + 0.35 + 0.15 + 0.05 = 1.0. The additive heads expose genuine partial progress while the common symmetry operator prevents incoherent basis/HKL mixing. Calibration cannot earn credit without lattice quality. Wrong/reordered columns, duplicate IDs, or an ID-set mismatch are rejected; malformed row JSON scores zero for that row. Dataset The public split has 1,920 labeled training packets and 480 hidden-test packets. Each row represents one event; related events are kept together during splitting, and public packets contain no original source identifiers. Probe IDs always refer to target-lattice spots in that packet. Distractor identities are not disclosed. details.title: Crystallographic Chain-Copy Assembly Synthesis
details.description:
Crystallographic Chain-Copy Assembly Synthesis Overview Proteins are three-dimensional molecular machines. In crystallography, scientists usually deposit an asymmetric unit, while the biologically relevant assembly may require copies of one or more chains transformed by crystallographic symmetry operators. Each operator is an affine transformation consisting of a 3 by 3 rotation matrix and a three-value translation vector. This challenge uses experimentally determined protein structures. Each public row is an anonymized, row-local assembly case containing compact chain geometry, a shuffled bank of non-identity affine-operator candidates, and noisy candidate contacts between possible transformed chain copies. Native entry identifiers and filenames are absent. The original asymmetric-unit copy is represented by the fixed identity transform BASE; it is always available and is not a scored operator choice. Your task is direct assembly synthesis. Infer which row-local chains participate, which operators generate their biological copies, and which transformed copies form the final interface graph. The complete executable construction must be inferred from the structural evidence itself. Task For every test row, submit: assembly_program_json: the selected local source chains and non-identity operator ids; interface_graph_json: the undirected contact graph induced by those chain copies; ambiguity_json: an uncertainty bucket for near-equivalent structural alternatives; confidence: confidence in the complete row prediction. The assembly program and graph are evaluated separately and jointly. A plausible graph does not identify the operators that generated it, while a plausible operator set may still induce the wrong contacts. Strong solutions must couple affine geometry, chain shape, contact evidence, and global graph consistency. Generalization Contract Train and test are split by source-family signatures before public ids are assigned. Related source families are kept in one partition, and rows are sorted only by opaque ids. The hidden set contains 280 nonempty assembly cases spanning independent families and varied chain, operator, and graph sizes. Candidate operators are bounded, perturbed rigid transforms containing native-selected and physically plausible alternative generators. Candidate contact features are noisy, incomplete, and quantized; their support values are evidence features, not the grader's hidden interface rule. Difficulty therefore comes from selecting a globally coherent chain/operator construction under family-disjoint generalization, not from an exposed threshold or arbitrary grading penalty. Intended Approach And Allowed Methods Strong From Scratch solutions can train directly on public/train.csv. Useful approaches include: graph or set encoders over chain, operator, and candidate-contact objects; learned scoring of chain/operator pairs using transformed coordinate summaries and the implicit BASE copy; pairwise contact models followed by constrained decoding of one executable assembly program; compact message-passing networks, transformer-style set encoders, ExtraTrees, gradient boosting, or hybrid geometric search; train-only family-aware validation for thresholds, decoding constraints, and confidence calibration. This is a CPU-based challenge. Solutions must fit within 10 CPU cores, 62.5 GB RAM, and 1.5 hours. NumPy, pandas, scikit-learn, CPU-mode PyTorch/JAX/TensorFlow, LightGBM/XGBoost, and custom graph decoding are appropriate. What Not To Use Using any of the following approaches is grounds for rejection on review: source-entry lookup, geometry fingerprinting against public structure archives, native-id recovery, filename matching, or source-manifest joins; row order, opaque-id hashes, CSV or JSON lengths, file sizes, archive metadata, or other non-physical side channels; hard-coded id-to-answer maps, private-file access, answer-key probing, grader exploitation, or manual hidden-test labeling; generic classification or regression that ignores the coupled assembly-program and graph object; graph-only or operator-only submissions presented as a complete solution; hosted closed-source APIs or external services during training or inference. Enforcement on Invalid Approaches: submissions may be rejected before payout when their primary method bypasses row-local structural inference through lookup, hidden-data access, metadata shortcuts, or platform exploitation. Evaluation For each row, the grader parses the two lists in assembly_program_json and computes: chain_score = set F1 on selected_asym_ids operator_score = set F1 on non-identity oper_expression program_score = 0.30chain_score + 0.70operator_score graph_score = set F1 on interface_graph_json edges ambiguity_score = 1 - abs(bucket_distance(pred, true)) / 3 compound = 1 if program, graph, and ambiguity all match exactly, else 0 Row correctness is: correctness = 0.42*program_score 0.50*graph_score 0.04*ambiguity_score 0.04*compound These four weights sum to exactly 1.0. Calibration is 1 - abs(confidence - correctness), and: row_score = 0.99correctness + 0.01calibration The final score blends global performance with hidden subgroup robustness: Final = 0.72 * mean(row_score) 0.18 * worst_family_mean(row_score) 0.10 * worst_complexity_mean(row_score) Higher is better. The theoretical minimum is 0.0; a perfect valid submission with confidence 1.0 scores exactly 1.0. Submission-level structural failures raise InvalidSubmissionError: missing, extra, or reordered columns; duplicate, missing, or extra ids; id-set mismatch; and non-finite or out-of-range confidence. Row-local JSON longer than 200,000 characters or malformed row-local values score zero for that row without exposing private information. Dataset The public dataset contains 1,079 labeled training rows and 280 hidden-test rows. Every row is one anonymized assembly-synthesis case with at least one native non-identity generator and at least one induced interface edge. Every graph node must use a submitted chain and either BASE or a submitted non-identity operator; an inconsistent row scores zero. ambiguity_json is an object whose required submission field is bucket, one of low, medium, high, or critical. details.title: Cross-Era Map Partial Correspondence
details.description:
# Cross-Era Map Partial Correspondence Overview Recover a partial one-to-one correspondence between labeled positions on a stylized historical map and anonymized clue tiles from a separately rendered archival-image channel. Only a subset of historical anchors has a candidate counterpart, and many candidate tiles are hard negatives that must be reported as unmatched. Each row supplies one map image, exact normalized positions for row-local historical IDs such as H03, and a set of row-local candidate IDs such as M08. Candidate evidence is visual rather than geometric: the candidate record identifies a tile in clue_sheets.npy, but contains no candidate coordinate, distance signature, global coordinate, source ID, seed match, or target match count. A correct solution must learn cross-domain visual similarity, reject plausible nearby negatives, and decide which anchors have no counterpart. This is a from-scratch multimodal structured-matching task. It is not coordinate registration, latitude/longitude prediction, source retrieval, or map-category classification. Only CPU solutions are allowed. The runtime limit is 1.5 hours on 10 CPU cores with 62 GB RAM. The full clue tensor is uint8 and can be memory-mapped with NumPy. Task For every test row, predict: matches_json: one-to-one {historical_id, modern_id} pairs. unmatched_modern_json: candidate IDs whose clue tiles do not correspond to any historical anchor in that row. confidence: finite row confidence in 0,1]. The map coordinates locate the Hxx anchors. Candidate identity must come from its clue tile. The clue channel is generated independently from the archival scan, while the public map uses a different stylized rendering. Clues vary in crop scale, tone, edge mixture, polarity, mirror/flip, anisotropic affine shear, rotation up to 30 degrees, resampling, and occluder position/shape. Distractors are real same-map patches, mostly sampled near annotated anchors, not artificial noise. Do not assume every historical anchor has a match. anchor_count and candidate_count describe the two input sets; neither reveals how many pairs belong in matches_json. Historical anchors without a counterpart are represented by omission from matches_json. Every candidate omitted from the predicted pairs should appear in unmatched_modern_json. Intended Approach A strong CPU solution can memory-map clue_sheets.npy, extract multi-scale map patches around each Hxx, and learn a compact cross-domain pair scorer from released rows. Useful inputs include gradient-orientation histograms, local keypoint geometry, frequency/texture summaries, and a small Siamese or metric-learning network trained from scratch. Train on both random and near-anchor hard negatives. At inference, augment the pairwise score matrix with dummy/unmatched states or apply a validation-calibrated rejection threshold before partial Hungarian assignment. Use grouped validation by source map or visually related sheet family. Compact CNNs trained only on released rows are allowed. A classical local-feature pipeline remains a useful baseline, but exhaustive pixel correlation plus forced full assignment is intentionally insufficient. Evaluation Higher is better. The theoretical range is exactly [0,1], and a perfect valid submission with confidence 1.0 scores exactly 1.0. For each row: S_match = F1 over exact (historical_id, modern_id) pairs S_unknown = F1 over unmatched candidate IDs core = 0.82 × S_match + 0.18 × S_unknown cal = max(0, 1 - abs(confidence - core)) row_score = 0.95 × core + 0.05 × cal The final score is: Final = 0.85 * mean(row_score) 0.15 * min(mean(row_score) for each hidden geographic region) The hidden geographic groups are physical regions derived from the source map's human GCP geography. The held-out split contains multiple regions and keeps every source map and related map-sheet family wholly in one split. Split Design and Limitations The deterministic split uses 79 source maps from 67 visually related sheet families for 1,027 training rows and holds out 34 source maps from 28 different families for 442 evaluation rows. No source map or related sheet family crosses the split, so repeated editions and visually similar sheets cannot leak from public training data into evaluation. The held-out rows span five physical geographic regions with 143, 26, 26, 195, and 52 rows; the worst-region term therefore measures performance on every region rather than only the largest groups. The corpus is not globally representative. Its five regions are imbalanced, some publishers and historical map styles are more common than others, and 79 public source maps cannot expose every scan condition present in held-out families. The fixed 640-pixel map scale and deterministic transformation ranges model a bounded matching problem rather than every form of real archival degradation. Solvers should group validation by source map or related sheet family and expect performance to vary with typography, cartographic density, aging, and scan quality. Every term is bounded and monotonic. Adding a correct pair, removing an incorrect pair, improving the unmatched set, or moving confidence closer to row correctness cannot lower the score when other predictions are fixed. There is no threshold cap, exponent, hidden cliff, exact-recovery multiplier, or global residual-error penalty. Malformed row-local JSON, repeated local IDs, unknown local IDs, or assigning a candidate as both matched and unmatched gives zero for that row. Wrong or reordered columns, missing/extra/duplicate test IDs, nonnumeric or non-finite confidence, confidence outside [0,1], unreadable CSV, or oversized input raises InvalidSubmissionError. Source and Attribution Anchor locations derive from human-created ground control points in the official Allmaps open-data snapshot. Historical map images come from the official IIIF manifests and image services listed in the approved dataset's SOURCE_MANIFEST.json. Allmaps annotation metadata is CC0 1.0; individual image rights comprise 109 Public Domain Mark 1.0 records, three CC BY 4.0 records, and one CC BY 3.0 record. Cite Allmaps and the corresponding IIIF providers/manifests when discussing or redistributing derived artifacts. Each sheet has four tile columns and four padded tile rows. Do not use original filenames, source IDs, collection IDs, raw URLs, hashes, file sizes, mtimes, row order, or ID decoding as answer channels. details.title: Bimanual Contact-Change Field From RGB Motion Pairs
details.description:
Bimanual Contact-Change Field From RGB Motion Pairs Overview The objective is to recover a signed bimanual contact-change field from an observed RGB motion pair. Each row contains two anonymized RGB frames from the same hand-object manipulation recording: a past frame and a current target frame. The model must infer how tactile glove pressure changed between those two visible moments. For each hand, submit a six-value calibrated pressure-delta vector in region order: thumb, index, middle, ring, little, palm. Values are in [-1,1] and represent current region mean pressure minus past region mean pressure. Also submit the contact-delta state for the observed interval, the target-frame peak pressure, and a confidence score. This is not object/action naming and not current-frame pressure-map reconstruction. A model should use both RGB frames to learn motion, hand posture change, contact geometry, and tool/object state cues that explain measured tactile change. The source sensors are real tactile gloves; the scored deltas and target-frame peak are derived directly from synchronized glove readings at the two visible frames. The key learning object is the residual contact field: which hand regions loaded, unloaded, or stayed stable over the visible interval. Existing static visuotactile tasks usually align one RGB frame with one absolute tactile snapshot; this challenge instead scores signed pressure redistribution across two RGB frames, hand-balance change, interval state, and target-frame peak contact. A static pressure predictor or action classifier is therefore incomplete unless it also learns the observed contact change. The split is grouped by complete source recording/task before any frame pair is exported: all frame pairs from a source episode stay entirely in train or entirely in test, and temporal neighbors never cross the boundary. Public ids are salted and shuffled, public image filenames contain only opaque row ids plus a past/current suffix, and source task names, frame indices, timestamps, raw paths, object/action labels, and pressure-derived grouping metadata are removed from public test inputs. The hidden test set covers held-out recordings across cutting, drilling, screw/unscrew, syringe, and water-pouring families, so the intended generalization is from visual contact-change patterns in training recordings to unseen recordings rather than memorizing adjacent frames. A residual risk is that determined solvers might try to reverse-match images against the public upstream videos; that is explicitly prohibited and the exported images are lightly normalized/cropped to reduce direct source lookup while preserving the RGB tactile-delta task. What Not To Use (any of these can cause solution rejection regardless of leaderboard score): Filename, row-order, EXIF, file-size, image-compression, or filesystem metadata side channels. Original source task names, source frame indices, timestamps, raw paths, or attempts to reverse-match public images to the upstream videos. Hard-coded answer dictionaries, private-file probes, grader/platform exploitation, or lookup tables built from hidden answers. Metadata-only approaches that ignore the RGB frame pair. Object/action naming as a substitute for bimanual contact-change recovery. Constant-output, majority-prior, nearest-row memorization, or template-inversion systems that do not learn visual contact change. Hosted or closed-source APIs at training or inference time, including distillation or pseudo-labeling from those systems. Extra columns, reordered columns, duplicate ids, invalid state values, out-of-range confidence, or malformed vectors intended to exploit the grader. Enforcement on invalid approaches: rule-only solutions, source-retrieval systems, metadata-only submissions, private-data access, or submissions that do not solve the RGB-to-contact-change task may be rejected before payout. The goal is to reward learned estimation of tactile change from RGB motion, not score-chasing shortcuts. Evaluation Each row is scored in [0,1]. The grader first checks the submission structure. Wrong/reordered columns, duplicate ids, id-set mismatch, invalid contact_delta_state, or invalid confidence raise an invalid-submission error. Row-local malformed pressure-delta vectors or malformed target_peak_pressure score zero for that row without revealing labels. For a valid row, the submitted left/right six-region delta vectors are concatenated and compared with the true current-minus-past tactile deltas. The independent delta score combines scaled MAE with weight 0.18, scaled RMSE with weight 0.10, correlation with weight 0.12, signed event F1 with weight 0.30, hand-balance agreement with weight 0.10, contact-delta-state agreement with weight 0.15, and target-peak-pressure agreement with weight 0.05. Row correctness is 88% independent delta score plus 12% joint signed-event/state/peak agreement. Calibration is 1 - abs(confidence - correctness). The row score is 95% correctness plus 5% calibration. The final score is 70% mean row score plus worst-group terms: task family 8%, dominant delta hand 8%, target pressure band 8%, and delta magnitude band 6%. Hidden subgroup axes are private and correspond to real task family, dominant changing hand, target-frame pressure magnitude, and tactile change magnitude. Higher is better. Theoretical minimum is 0.0; theoretical maximum is 1.0. Perfect labels with confidence 1.0 score exactly 1.0. details.title: FiberCharge: Optical-Electrical Retired Battery Reconstruction
details.description:
Objective Domain: Multimodal sensor fusion. This is not a tabular prediction task: train.csv and test.csv are manifests, while the model inputs are paired optical and electrical waveform arrays stored in per-episode .npz packets. Every solution must learn from both sensing modalities. This is a multimodal sensor-fusion reconstruction challenge. Reconstruct the chemistry, state of health, complete-discharge response, and missing optical response of a retired battery cell from compact paired optical/electrical diagnostic packets. Each row is one measured 180-second episode. The corpus contains exactly twelve non-overlapping episodes per physical cell, and every scored target is measured from that same cell and episode. For each test episode_id, predict: chemistry: LFP or LMO. soh: measured state of health. capacity_q00 through capacity_q23: discharge voltage response. optical_q00 through optical_q31: withheld optical deltas. Task Load the .npz packet referenced by each row of test.csv. Treat its fixed-length arrays as a structured multimodal feature vector and learn jointly from the 91 aligned voltage, current, observed optical, and mask values. The optical values at feature coordinates corresponding to 60 through 122 seconds are withheld and scored at their original two-second resolution. Use the opaque cell_group_id to pool the twelve episodes from the same physical cell. The public arrays preserve source-faithful measurement precision; source names, timestamps, and source row order are removed. The split is deterministic at the physical-cell level: all twelve episodes from a cell appear in exactly one of train or test, with chemistry and SOH-band stratification, so no measurement from a held-out cell occurs in training. The prepared corpus has 2,004 training episodes from 167 cells and 1,152 test episodes from 96 held-out cells. Test visibility is independently balanced within chemistry/SOH strata (48 public and 48 private cells, including 5 public and 5 private LMO-mid cells). Opaque IDs are salted hashes unrelated to source identity, output order is hash-shuffled, and filenames, timestamps, source row order, and path metadata are removed. All 3,156 retained packets are unique, and no test packet exactly matches any training packet, preventing pattern lookup or cell fingerprinting from substituting for learned sensor fusion. Intended Approaches Use a compact CPU model such as a residual MLP, cross-channel attention encoder, tree ensemble over engineered packet features, or an ensemble of these. Optical-only, electrical-only, constant-prior, and interpolation-only models are useful ablations, but competitive solutions should fuse both modalities and model all continuous heads. Compute Contract CPU only: 10 cores, 62 GiB RAM, and at most 1.5 hours. Use packages and model weights available offline before the run. Runtime downloads, hosted inference, private files, and remote APIs are forbidden. What Not To Use Original-source lookup or fingerprinting. Source names, IDs, paths, or timestamps. File size, hash, mtime, or row-order attacks. Private files or fixed answer dictionaries. Hosted APIs or runtime downloads. Grader parsing or range exploits. Submissions may be reviewed for source lookup, external calls, metadata-only behavior, or approaches that avoid the multimodal reconstruction task. Data Prepared files are under public/. Voltage deltas use 0.001 V precision, normalized current uses 0.01 precision, and observed optical deltas use 0.00001 nm precision. Masked optical values are zero only where the mask is zero. Submission Format Submit one row per test ID, in exactly this order: episode_id,chemistry,soh,capacity_q00,...,capacity_q23,optical_q00,...,optical_q31 | Column | Type | Constraint | |---|---|---| | episode_id | string | Exact test ID set | | chemistry | enum | LFP or LMO | | soh | float | [0.40, 1.10] | | capacity_qNN | float | [2.0, 4.3] V | | optical_qNN | float | [-0.10, 0.10] nm | Evaluation Higher is better. For each episode: chemistry_score = exact match soh_score = max(0, 1 - abs(error) / 0.030) capacity_score = mean(max(0, 1 - abs(error) / 0.040)) optical_score = mean(max(0, 1 - abs(error) / 0.0012)) balance_score = min(soh_score, capacity_score, optical_score) row_score = 0.10chemistry_score + 0.30soh_score 0.12capacity_score + 0.18optical_score 0.30*balance_score cell_score = mean(row_score over the cell's 12 episodes) final_score = mean(cell_score over the 96 held-out physical cells) The 0.30 balance_score is an intentional joint-task bottleneck: without it, a solver can earn a strong score by optimizing SOH while largely ignoring either the complete-discharge or withheld-optical reconstruction head. details.description:
Overview A chemical-monitoring rig has lost its controller log, but the multichannel response traces from each exposure remain. Recover the ordered two-stage exposure program from every hidden sensor sequence: dose state first, then moisture state. This is a multiclass sequence-classification task with one joint program label per exposure.   Each example is a 256-step, 6-channel float32 sequence from one continuous physical exposure. The first three channels are lower, median, and upper response trajectories across an anonymous sensor set. The final three channels are their first-difference trajectories. Evaluation examples come from unseen acquisition conditions with local calibration and timing variation. The legal program grammar is exactly Cnn>Hmm. The dose token is one of C00, C01, C02, C03, or C04; the moisture token is one of H00, H01, H02, or H03. C03>H02 is valid. Both stages must be recovered in the stated order. Task Load each sequence named in train.csv, train a sequence classifier on exposure_program, and predict one valid program for every ID in test.csv. Intended Approach Use the full temporal tensor. Compact 1D CNNs, temporal convolutional networks, recurrent models, and small Transformers trained from scratch are suitable. A multi-task model may use separate dose and moisture heads plus a joint-program head. details.title: Cell Event Program Recovery from Fluorescence Traces
details.description:
Cell Event Program Recovery from Fluorescence Traces Overview Each row contains a short anonymized sensor log from a real yeast cell experiment. Think of it as a multivariate time series: for each observed cell, you receive one value sequence for brightness, one value sequence for cell size, and a validity mask that says which frames are usable. Your task is to predict the ordered event list hidden in that time series. For each cell, identify whether and when two event types happen: bud_onset, meaning a visible growth event starts, and trace_exit, meaning the tracked cell leaves or ends before the recording finishes. This challenge belongs to the From Scratch domain. Participants may train models on the supplied public training rows, but may not use hosted inference, GPU-only workflows, private files, or external source lookup. Dataset The public data is derived from real cell-cycle microscopy experiments. The raw upload contains microscope image examples, cell-tracking resources, MATLAB analysis files, and per-cell trace files. The challenge input is a prepared trace packet, not the raw images. For each example, open the row's manifest_path. The manifest has this structure: { "id": "Y123EXAMPLE", "frame_count": 120, "cells": [ { "cell_id": "C1A2B3C4D", "fluorescence": [0.13, 0.20, -0.05], "relative_area": [0.98, 1.01, 1.04], "valid": [1, 1, 1] } ] } frame_count is the number of time steps. Each item in cells is one tracked cell. fluorescence is the normalized brightness sequence, relative_area is the normalized size sequence, and valid is a same-length 0/1 mask. cell_id is an anonymized handle that must be reused exactly in predictions for that row. train.csv has id, manifest_path, prompt, and target_json. test.csv has the same input columns without target_json. sample_submission.csv has the required submission header and held-out ID order. details.title: Coupled Pendulum Hidden Coupling-Graph Inference
details.description:
Coupled Pendulum Hidden Coupling-Graph Inference Overview Infer which pendulums influence one another from their motion in a short video, identify the strongest coupling, and predict each pendulum's phase well after the recording. The data are fully synthetic: a linear small-angle coupled-oscillator model is rendered as a head-on view of eight to ten pendulums on a shared rail. This is an idealized system-identification task, not footage of physical experiments. Every bob has the same size and colour and displays an integer ID from 0 to n_pendulums-1. Hidden links are never drawn. IDs and horizontal positions do not indicate the coupling graph. Use the motion over time to distinguish direct coupling from coincidental or indirect correlation. The coupling graph is undirected; its coefficients describe symmetric interactions. Return the coupled pairs, the pair with the largest coupling coefficient, a phase for every printed ID at query_time_s, and a confidence estimate of your weighted prediction accuracy. Strongest coupling means largest model coefficient; it is not necessarily the pair with the largest observed amplitude change. Some links are harder to estimate from short observations, but no unmeasured irreducible performance ceiling is claimed. Phase is atan2(angular_velocity / natural_angular_frequency, angle), converted to degrees modulo 360. Angle is zero when vertical and positive toward the right side of the displayed image; angular velocity uses the same sign. Natural angular frequency is the pendulum's uncoupled frequency, which must be inferred. Forecast the displayed motion, including the sign shown in mirrored views, and always answer using printed IDs. You may train visual and relational models or fit motion and coupled dynamics statistically. Estimate model choices from the labelled training data. Stream videos and retain compact trajectories rather than loading the corpus into memory. Compute and runtime Target CPU runtime: up to 10 cores and 62.5 GiB RAM, approximately one hour for the complete solution. No GPU or runtime internet is required or permitted by this challenge. Use standard Kaggle Python Docker libraries. Read only ./dataset/public/ and write generated files under ./working/, ending with ./working/submission.csv. A practical CPU route is video tracking followed by a fitted dynamics model or a lightweight learned graph model. What Not To Use Do not use hosted model APIs, runtime downloads, external copies of these clips, or external answer lookups. Do not access private files, raw simulator metadata, generation seeds, or organizer scripts. Do not exploit filenames, row order, filesystem metadata, grading internals, or hard-coded answer dictionaries. Do not replace the required outputs with captions or a different prediction task. A single frame, fixed graph, or ID-adjacency rule is only a weak diagnostic, not evidence of recovered dynamics. Relation to prior work Neural Relational Inference (Kipf et al., 2018) studies latent interaction graphs from trajectories; Visual Causal Discovery Network (Li et al., 2020) also studies visual interaction discovery and dynamics prediction. This challenge uses printed-ID pendulum videos, short observation windows, and long-horizon phase forecasts. It shares the broader inference objective with that literature. Evaluation Higher is better. Scores range from 0.0 to 1.0. Each clip has three accuracy components: E = 2 * |predicted_edges intersect true_edges| / (|predicted_edges| + |true_edges|) S = 1 for the exact strongest pair, otherwise 0 P = mean_i exp(-circular_distance(predicted_phase_i, true_phase_i) / 30) C = 0.50E + 0.22S + 0.28*P A = 1 - abs(confidence - C) row_score = C * (0.90 + 0.10*A) final_score = mean(row_score over all test clips) The weighting expresses the task priorities: half the credit rewards recovery of the full interaction graph, 22% rewards identifying its single strongest link, and 28% tests whether the inferred dynamics support future phase prediction. This gives graph structure the majority (72%) while retaining a substantial forecasting test; the weights are task-design choices, not physical constants or estimates fitted to baseline scores. Strongest-pair accuracy measures a specific interaction that aggregate edge F1 can miss. The 30-degree phase scale gives credit of exp(-1) at a one-twelfth-cycle error and smooth partial credit as errors decrease. Confidence is a self-estimate of C: absolute error gives a bounded, interpretable penalty, and its 10% modulation keeps prediction quality dominant. This is an accuracy-estimation term, not a claim of probabilistic calibration or a proper scoring rule. For a fixed C, matching confidence to C maximizes row credit. Two valid empty edge sets have E=1. If only one is empty, E=0. A true empty strongest-pair label matches only a well-formed []. A malformed strongest pair has S=0, including for no-edge rows. Phase distance is the shorter distance around the circle, from 0 to 180 degrees. Finite phase numbers are wrapped modulo 360. A missing or invalid phase value contributes zero for that pendulum; an unparseable phase object, duplicate JSON key, or impossible ID makes the phase head zero. Confidence estimates C, not the probability that every target is exactly correct. It adjusts earned accuracy and never supplies credit for wholly wrong predictions. No hidden subgroup weight, score cap, or score power is applied. The exact five submission columns and their order are required. Missing, extra, reordered or duplicate columns; duplicate, missing, extra or fractional row IDs; and nonnumeric, nonfinite, boolean or out-of-range confidence make the submission score 0.0. Legitimate numeric-string row IDs are accepted. Malformed row-local predictions affect their corresponding accuracy head without discarding valid predictions in other rows or heads. JSON cells are limited to 20,000 characters and four nesting levels before decoding. Pair endpoints must be JSON integers in 0..n_pendulums-1, distinct and valid. Reversed pair order is accepted; duplicate edges, self-loops, fractional/boolean/quoted endpoints, impossible IDs and invalid pair shapes make that graph head zero. Phases must be JSON numbers, not booleans or quoted strings. Nonstandard NaN/Infinity JSON tokens and duplicate object keys are invalid. Dataset There are 1311 labelled training clips and 639 test clips. Every video is a 1280 x 360 H.264 MP4 containing 24 RGB frames at 12 fps. # Biofouling Crowd Consensus Calibration Overview Each row contains one 256 by 256 privacy-preserving inspection mosaic assembled from four underwater frames collected during the same vessel inspection. Four deterministic crops are sampled from each frame, transformed, shuffled, and arranged as a 4 by 4 grid of 16 tiles. Predict how a population of human inspectors distributes its ratings among three ordered biofouling states: clean, patchy, and heavy. The training targets preserve disagreement instead of collapsing it to a majority label. Each mosaic target is the arithmetic mean of the four component frames' empirical rating distributions. Most source frames have nine independent ratings; three exact-duplicate source pairs were consolidated transparently and have 18 retained ratings under one canonical frame. A prediction such as [0.50, 0.35, 0.15] means that a randomly selected rating distribution represented by the panel is expected to be clean, patchy, or heavy with those probabilities. This is a From Scratch computer-vision calibration task. It is not ordinary hard-label classification, source identification, image retrieval, or expert adjudication. The hidden split holds out complete vessel families, and privacy processing removes full-frame layout and public-source identifiers. The held-out families are selected deterministically to preserve aggregate label, entropy, source-collection, and coarse visual distributions while keeping every family and near-duplicate-connected unit on only one side of the split. Models must learn texture, coating condition, fouling coverage, and ambiguity directly from the mosaics. There are 944 training mosaics and 338 hidden-test mosaics. Training and test use disjoint vessel families, with near-duplicate-connected families kept together. Public rows contain no vessel ID, original filename, source collection, raw order, annotator ID, or individual vote record. Both splits include an opaque cv_group that reveals only within-split validation co-membership; it must be excluded from model features, and no group value crosses the hidden split. Task For every test ID, submit exactly three probabilities: p_clean: probability of no visible macrofouling, although biofilm or slime may be present. p_patchy: probability of visible but patchy macrofouling. p_heavy: probability of extensive macrofouling. Every value must be finite and in [0,1], and the three values in each row must sum to one within 1e-6. Intended Approach Train a compact image model from scratch on the supplied mosaics and soft labels. A small residual CNN, patch encoder with attention pooling, or convolutional texture network can produce three logits followed by softmax. Optimize Brier loss or cross-entropy against the soft target distributions. Use cv_group with a grouped or stratified-grouped splitter because neighboring panels from one inspection share visual style; never pass cv_group into the model as a feature. Color/texture features with a tree regressor provide a weak CPU baseline, while a compact CNN can model localized fouling patterns and disagreement. Calibration should be validated directly: predicting only the majority class discards the signal being scored. The official environment is CPU-only with 10 cores, 62 GB RAM, and a 1.5-hour end-to-end limit. Runtime internet access is not allowed. The corpus is small enough for compact from-scratch training and full inference within that budget. What Not To Use Do not identify, download, or match the upstream source images or annotations. Do not reverse the privacy mosaic, recover component frames, or use external source labels. Do not use released upstream models, pretrained image encoders, foundation-model embeddings, hosted vision APIs, or runtime downloads. Do not use filenames, row order, file bytes, opaque-ID hashes, cv_group, source reconstruction, or hidden split metadata as prediction features. Do not access private answers, grader internals, organizer files, or any non-public path. Do not submit fixed priors, rule-only lookup tables, hard-label-only outputs, or other approaches that avoid learning the image-to-distribution task. Do not exploit duplicate IDs, missing rows, reordered columns, NaN/Inf values, out-of-range values, or non-unit probability sums. Approaches that use source lookup, external/pretrained models, private data, or do not align with from-scratch image learning may be rejected before payout. Evaluation The Crowd Distribution Skill Score is maximized and lies in [0,1]. For test row i, let the prediction be q_i=(q_clean,q_patchy,q_heavy) and the hidden empirical distribution be p_i. The mean three-class Brier loss is: BS = mean_i sum_c (q_i,c - p_i,c)^2 The fixed reference BS_ref = 0.11676673729921867 is computed only from training-label dispersion around the training climatology. The final score is: raw_fidelity = max(0, 1 - BS/2) skill = max(0, 1 - BS/BS_ref) score = 0.15raw_fidelity + 0.85skill A perfect submission scores exactly 1.0. The supplied train-prior sample scores about 0.157. Wrong or reordered columns, duplicate IDs, a missing/extra/foreign ID, a nonnumeric or nonfinite probability, a value outside [0,1], or a row whose probabilities do not sum to one raises InvalidSubmissionError and rejects the submission. details.description:
Overview At the close of each half-hour electricity-market planning window, a system operator sees hundreds of generating and demand-side units, each with a submitted physical plan, operating limits, and a ladder of bid/offer prices and levels. The operator may then accept a variable portfolio of actions: increase some units, decrease others, issue instructions at different times, and revise the physical target trajectory within the period. For each real operational planning episode, predict that complete portfolio. This is not a scalar price forecast and not an independent yes/no classification of one candidate. One output row is an ordered, variable-length JSON list of unit/direction action choices. Every chosen action also needs its instruction time and accepted physical-level trajectory. The candidate universe is provided as a compressed NumPy set. Candidate IDs are episode-local and opaque. Stable pseudonymous unit tokens let a model learn a unit's behavior across training episodes without exposing the upstream unit name. All physical values are MW and all bid/offer prices are GBP/MWh. Task For every test episode: decide which candidate action_id values are accepted; estimate the first instruction time in minutes relative to period start; estimate the accepted absolute physical level over one or more within-period trajectory segments; and order non-concurrent actions by predicted instruction time. An offer means increasing net generation or reducing demand, represented by direction = +1. A bid means decreasing net generation or increasing demand, represented by direction = -1. Accepted levels are absolute target physical levels, not changes from zero. Use pn_mean_mw, the supplied pre-decision trajectory summaries, and the direction when reasoning about action magnitude. Training rows include the full target portfolio_json. Test rows include only their candidate archive. Learn one model from the supplied training set and produce one portfolio per test ID. This is a From Scratch challenge. Model weights must be randomly initialized and trained only on the supplied public training data. The requested platform tier is one NVIDIA A10G GPU. The runtime budget is 90 minutes with 10 CPU cores and 62 GB RAM. A small set/candidate encoder plus an autoregressive or ranking-and-regression head is sufficient; giant foundation models are neither needed nor allowed. The recorded dispatch is not claimed to be the unique solution of a fully observed optimization problem. Network, security, reserve, and operator constraints are not all present in these feeds. The learning goal is the historical conditional distribution of recorded actions, and the metric gives partial credit for correct portfolio members, time, trajectory, and order. Public files | Item | Description | |---|---| | train.csv | labeled training episodes | | test.csv | unlabeled test episodes | | sample_submission.csv | valid learned train-prior submission and exact CSV/JSON schema | | train/*.npz | candidate-set tensors for training episodes | | test/*.npz | candidate-set tensors for test episodes | | DATA_README.md | compact loading note | The final frozen split has 764 training periods from 16 contiguous days and 240 test periods from five later contiguous days. IDs are salted and source-neutral. CSV files are sorted by ID; row order carries no chronology. An opaque day_group token identifies same-day training examples so validation folds can keep whole days together without revealing dates or their order. CSV columns train.csv: | Column | Type | Description | |---|---|---| | id | string | opaque episode ID | | day_group | string | opaque same-day group for leakage-safe validation | | episode_path | string | relative path to one training NPZ | | portfolio_json | string | canonical target action portfolio | test.csv: | Column | Type | Description | |---|---|---| | id | string | opaque episode ID | | day_group | string | opaque same-day group; values never overlap training | | episode_path | string | relative path to one test NPZ | Load an episode with numpy.load(path, allow_pickle=False). Each NPZ contains: | Key | Shape/type | Description | |---|---|---| | features | [n_candidates, 29] float32 | candidate feature matrix | | candidate_ids | [n_candidates] Unicode | legal action_id values for this row | | unit_tokens | [n_candidates] Unicode | stable pseudonymous unit identities | | directions | [n_candidates] int8 | +1 offer or -1 bid | | context | [6] float32 | period and system context | | feature_names | [29] Unicode | column names for features | | context_names | [6] Unicode | element names for context | The 29 candidate features, in order, are: direction, pn_mean_mw, pn_start_mw, pn_end_mw, pn_range_mw, mel_max_mw, mil_min_mw, headroom_mw, footroom_mw, directional_flex_mw, best_price_gbp_mwh, worst_price_gbp_mwh, weighted_price_gbp_mwh, available_pair_count, then five pair_k_capacity_mw fields, five pair_k_price_gbp_mwh fields, and five pair_k_available mask fields for k=1..5. The six context values are period_sin, period_cos, weekday_sin, weekday_cos, pn_system_total_gw, and candidate_flex_total_gw. Portfolio JSON schema portfolio_json is a JSON list with zero to 256 action objects. Every action has exactly these keys: { "action_id": "a_0123456789abcdef0123", "instruction_minute": -12.0, "trajectory": [ {"t0": 0.0, "t1": 12.0, "level0": 420.0, "level1": 420.0}, {"t0": 12.0, "t1": 30.0, "level0": 438.0, "level1": 438.0} ] } action_id must match one of the row's supplied candidate IDs and the grader requires the opaque format a_ plus 20 lowercase hexadecimal characters. instruction_minute is finite and lies in [-90, 30]. Negative values are valid instructions issued after the feature cutoff but before period start. trajectory contains 1–32 sorted, non-overlapping segments. Segment t0 and t1 are finite minutes with 0 <= t0 < t1 <= 30. level0 and level1 are finite absolute MW values in [-10000, 10000]. Actions are sorted by (instruction_minute, action_id). Repeated IDs are syntactically allowed, but the native target contains one consolidated action per unit/direction candidate. JSON is capped at 250,000 characters. Duplicate keys, extra keys, NaN, Infinity, and non-canonical list order are invalid. Submit a CSV with exactly id,portfolio_json, in that order. Include every test ID exactly once. File-level structural errors (wrong/reordered columns, duplicate IDs, missing/extra IDs) raise InvalidSubmissionError. A malformed JSON cell is row-local and scores zero for that row. What Not To Use Do not use external data, the internet, upstream-source or archive lookup, exact or fuzzy temporal fingerprinting, raw-record matching, source filenames, timestamps, modification times, file sizes, row/archive order, public test-label retrieval, hard-coded per-ID outputs, private answers, or any other side channel. Do not use pretrained weights, foundation-model embeddings, hosted/closed APIs, teacher-generated labels, pseudo-labels derived from hidden test outcomes, transductive access to test labels, or inference-only answer caches. Do not reduce the task to a constant portfolio, a fixed top-N merit-order rule, an ID/unit lookup table without learned market-state features, independent thresholding with no portfolio/count/order model, or a parser that copies a target-bearing field. Do not infer offer/bid direction by taking the sign of an accepted level relative to zero: accepted levels are absolute and direction is relative to the supplied pre-decision physical plan. Do not train on test periods or use post-cutoff, revised, corrected, deemed, or future action records. Allowed methods include randomly initialized neural set encoders, temporal models, candidate rankers, constrained decoders, ordinary loss functions and augmentations for numeric data, and classical features computed solely from the provided training inputs. Solutions must fit the stated A10G/CPU/RAM/time budget. Enforcement The grader enforces the complete CSV row set, exact columns/order, unique IDs, JSON length and object-count caps, duplicate-key rejection, finite numeric bounds, action/segment schemas, segment order, and canonical action order. Prohibited external lookup, pretrained models, answer retrieval, hard-coded test outputs, or future/corrected data remain grounds for rejection even when a submission is syntactically valid. Evaluation Actions are matchable only when action_id agrees. Repeated instances of the same ID are paired greedily by a similarity of 45% instruction time and 55% trajectory. For each row: | Component | Definition | Coefficient | |---|---|---| | Action multiset F1 | 2 × matched / (predicted_count + true_count) | 0.40 | | Instruction similarity | mean max(0, 1 - absolute_minute_error / 20) over matches | 0.15 | | Trajectory similarity | one-minute temporal IoU plus scale-aware absolute-level accuracy over matches | 0.25 | | Tie-aware ordering | concordant matched pairs; true instructions within one minute are ignored as ties | 0.15 | | Count similarity | 1 - abs(predicted_count - true_count) / max(predicted_count, true_count, 1) | 0.05 | Trajectory comparison samples minute midpoints. Its temporal term is the intersection-over-union of predicted and true covered minutes. On intersecting minutes, the level term is max(0, 1 - MAE / (2 × scale)), where scale = max(25, 0.15 × mean(abs(true_level)) + 25). Trajectory similarity is 0.45 × temporal_iou + 0.55 × temporal_iou × level_similarity. If both portfolios are empty, the row score is 1. If only one is empty, the row score is 0. Otherwise let F be action multiset F1 and define Q = 0.15 × instruction + 0.25 × trajectory + 0.15 × ordering. The row score is 0.40 × F + F × Q + 0.05 × count_similarity, clipped only for numerical safety to [0,1]. Attribute and order quality therefore earn credit in proportion to portfolio coverage: predicting one convenient action accurately cannot collect most of the time/trajectory/order credit while omitting the rest of the recorded dispatch. This is part of the task definition, not a score cap or post-hoc transformation. The overall score is the arithmetic mean over all private rows. A perfect submission scores exactly 1.0; the theoretical minimum is 0.0. Frozen full-split checks gave 1.000000 for exact answers and 0.000000 for no action. The generated learned sample scored 0.258693 and the deliberately weak frequency/merit CPU baseline scored 0.301272. A capability-matched portfolio baseline uses opaque-day grouped out-of-fold candidate probabilities, a learned episode action-count model, and learned instruction/trajectory heads; its frozen score is 0.373229, leaving substantial headroom to perfect. Data boundary The supplied inputs are anonymized, source-neutral candidate-set tensors created from pre-decision operational snapshots. Training targets are recorded post-cutoff action portfolios. The public package excludes raw identifiers, original names, absolute dates, filenames, external-location fields, and every target-bearing field. Solvers must train only on the provided public training files and must not retrieve or match against any external corpus. The final split is chronological by complete operating day: 16 complete days for training followed by five complete later days for private evaluation. No upstream record or episode crosses partitions. Public IDs and same-day group tokens are opaque and salted; the public files omit absolute timestamps, raw unit names, event identifiers, publication metadata, and all external-location fields.

## Overview Argo Delayed-Mode Ocean Profile QC Decisions This is a From Scratch scientific array-segmentation challenge. Ocean profiling floats report independent depth-indexed pressure, temperature, and salinity arrays. Expert operators later review suspicious profiles and change quality-control decisions over specific depth intervals. Every example in this challenge is known to contain at least one such expert action. Your task is to find the affected temperature or salinity intervals and predict the kind of QC transition the operator recorded. This is conditional action localization, not general screening of arbitrary ocean profiles and not prediction of the QC fields stored in a current NetCDF file. Participant inputs contain only normalized raw pressure, temperature, and salinity measurements plus validity masks. QC flags, adjusted values, calibration records, history records, source names, geographic coordinates, timestamps, and original identifiers are absent. Each example is a vertical spatial profile rather than a chronological forecasting series. All profiles from one physical float stay in one split. Test floats never occur in training, so successful solutions must learn transferable profile-shape and anomaly patterns rather than memorize a platform. What Not To Do Do not use the internet, external source files, source lookup, or hosted inference services. Do not reconstruct original float identifiers or match public arrays to outside Argo records. Do not infer answers from opaque IDs, row order, paths, array sizes, or file metadata. Do not submit a hand-coded threshold or lookup-only pipeline with no trained model. Do not use private files, hidden answers, grader internals, or repeated submissions as an answer-extraction channel. Do not use current QC, adjusted, calibration, or history fields; they are intentionally unavailable. Task For each test profile, load its n_levels by 6 NumPy array and predict non-overlapping inclusive intervals for TEMP and PSAL. Each predicted interval is [start_level, stop_level, class]. Transition classes are: class 1: QC 1 to 3; class 2: QC 1 to 4; class 3: any other recorded old-to-new transition. Levels not covered by a submitted interval mean no expert action for that parameter. Indices are zero-based and inclusive. Intended Approach And Validation A strong solution should train a GPU model such as a dilated 1D CNN, U-Net-style 1D segmenter, compact Transformer encoder, or boosted level predictor with multi-scale profile features. Useful features include local vertical gradients, robust rolling residuals, pressure-aware receptive fields, cross-parameter consistency, missingness masks, and multi-scale context. Predict per-level action classes, then merge adjacent equal nonzero predictions into intervals. Use series_id to create grouped validation folds so one float never appears in both sides of a validation split. Class weighting, focal loss, hard-negative mining, boundary-aware losses, and probability calibration are reasonable. Validate both event localization and transition identity; a model that predicts broad intervals will lose no-change accuracy and precision. The supplied reference uses GPU gradient-boosted level taggers with multi-scale profile features. It selects thresholds on a float-grouped public validation fold, trains from scratch on the released labels, and does not use pretrained weights or external data. Evaluation Scores are maximized. Every structurally valid test row receives: row_score = 0.15 * detection_accuracy 0.55 * event_f1 0.30 * transition_macro_f1 final_score = mean(row_score) detection_accuracy measures event versus no-event correctness across all TEMP and PSAL levels. event_f1 is binary F1 for corrected levels. transition_macro_f1 is macro F1 over transition classes present in the union of true and predicted event levels. This combination rewards precise boundaries and transition identity while penalizing broad or empty predictions. A perfect submission scores exactly 1.0. The theoretical range is 0.0 to 1.0. details.description:
Adaptive Demagnetization Program Recovery Overview Progressive demagnetization helps scientists separate magnetic remanence components carried by a rock specimen. Real specimens can contain several components whose coercivity or unblocking ranges overlap, while laboratory measurements may be sparse or contain isolated disturbances. For each simulated episode, you receive a 96-step sequence representing a completed pilot alternating-field or thermal experiment. Only a subset of the magnetic vectors is observed. The simulated material contains two to four components with different directions, release profiles, and relative weights. Recover a structured component program, identify one or two impulse artifacts, and select three additional treatment positions for a follow-up experiment on an idealized equivalent aliquot. The simulator assumes the replicate has the same component mixture and release curves. This is not a request to reverse treatment on a specimen that has already been demagnetized. The output is a finite-token structured record of component properties, artifacts, and follow-up treatment decisions. The central challenge is to learn vector-mixture decomposition and acquisition-policy imitation jointly from labelled examples. The reference treatment choices favor component-release contrast while retaining signal and avoiding redundant positions; they are simulator-policy labels, not a claim of experimentally proven optimal laboratory actions. The empirical release shapes are grounded in real public paleomagnetic laboratory measurements. Every challenge episode is newly composed with sampled component directions, weights, profile warps, observation masks, drift, noise, and impulse artifacts. Public rows carry opaque IDs and fixed-size arrays. They do not contain source contribution names, publication identifiers, specimen names, raw treatment values, source filenames, original row order, or hidden generator state. Do not reduce the task to one PCA line, one best-fit interval, magnitude-only interpolation, component-count classification, or next-step prediction alone. Do not submit hard-coded per-ID outputs, malformed or oversized JSON, duplicate IDs, missing rows, invalid token values, or non-finite confidence values. Task For every test row, load the sequence at sequence_row from sequences.npy and submit one program_json object plus confidence. Training and test rows reference the same shared tensor below the public data directory. Each tensor index identifies exactly one episode across both CSVs. The program has three fields: components: two to four component objects. Each object has direction, release, and weight integer tokens. artifacts: one or two objects of the form {"type":"SPIKE","bin":k}. next_treatments: three unique treatment-candidate tokens in increasing order. Component order is not scored; the grader finds the maximum-weight one-to-one matching. Artifact bins and next-treatment tokens must be unique and sorted. Input arrays and token dictionaries Each row selected from a public .npy tensor is a finite float32 array with shape [96,7]. Its columns are: column 0 treatment_fraction normalized treatment position from 0 to 1 column 1 observed_mask 1 when a magnetic vector is observed, else 0 column 2 protocol_code -1 for alternating-field, +1 for thermal column 3 mx normalized specimen-frame x component column 4 my normalized specimen-frame y component column 5 mz normalized specimen-frame z component column 6 magnitude norm of the observed magnetic vector At unobserved positions, mx, my, mz, and magnitude are zero. treatment_fraction, observed_mask, and protocol_code remain defined. Every scored impulse artifact occurs at an observed step. The 16 treatment-candidate positions are absent from the pilot observation mask and are available for the proposed follow-up experiment. The field name next_treatments refers to that follow-up schedule, not to positions after the final observed treatment on the original aliquot. direction is an integer from 0 through 47. The corresponding unit-vector centers are published in direction_centers.csv. release is an integer from 0 through 11. The half-release step is the earliest grid index whose component intensity is closest to the midpoint between its initial and final intensities. Token k means that step index falls in [8k, 8k+7]. This measures half of the total modeled drop, not necessarily a reduction to half the initial intensity. weight is an integer from 0 through 4. Token k represents the fifth of the unit interval containing the component's normalized mixture weight. Artifact bin is an integer from 1 through 14 on a 16-bin normalized treatment grid; bin k maps to sequence index round(95*k/15). Tokens 0 and 15 are not valid artifact positions. next_treatments uses integers from 0 through 15. The exact token-to-step and token-to-treatment mapping is published in treatment_candidates.csv, whose columns are treatment_index (integer category 0–15), step (integer sequence position), and treatment_fraction (normalized treatment level). These are scientific category indices, not authentication credentials. Intended approach and validation A strong solution should treat each row as a masked vector sequence. Suitable GPU approaches include a temporal convolutional network, a compact transformer encoder, a state-space sequence model, or a differentiable mixture-decomposition front end followed by multi-task classification heads. Useful augmentations include additional observation dropout, small vector noise, axis-preserving jitter, and training-only rotations that update direction targets consistently. One practical pipeline encodes the seven-channel sequence, predicts a latent episode representation, decodes component count and component tokens, then uses separate heads for artifact events and acquisition planning. A constrained decoder should remove padding slots, keep legal token ranges, choose unique treatment tokens, sort the two set-valued fields, and emit valid JSON. Use only public/train.csv and the referenced public arrays for model fitting. Create a held-out validation subset within the labeled training data, stratified by protocol and component count. Source-family identifiers are not available publicly, so do not assume exact source-grouped validation is possible. Monitor the complete metric rather than one head: component recovery, count, follow-up treatment planning, artifacts, and confidence calibration all contribute. The compact temporal convolutional reference fits on one A10G GPU. Permutation-aware decoding, explicit vector-mixture layers, and ensembles are approaches to investigate; improvement over the reference is not guaranteed. Simulator results are not validated for real laboratory-control decisions. Evaluation Scores are maximized. The theoretical minimum is 0.0 and a perfect submission scores exactly 1.0. The grader first validates the whole CSV. Wrong or reordered columns, missing rows, extra rows, duplicate IDs, foreign IDs, or an ID-set mismatch raise InvalidSubmissionError. The error is generic and does not reveal hidden labels, source identities, split logic, or row-level scores. Prediction-content failures are local to a row. Malformed or overlong JSON, illegal keys, wrong list lengths, invalid tokens, repeated or unsorted set tokens, or a nonnumeric, NaN, infinite, or out-of-range confidence value give only that row a score of zero. Other valid rows continue to be scored. For a predicted component and a true component: direction_credit = max(0, 1 - angular_error_degrees / 90) release_credit = max(0, 1 - abs(pred_release - true_release) / 6) weight_credit = max(0, 1 - abs(pred_weight - true_weight) / 4) pair_credit = 0.55direction_credit + 0.30release_credit + 0.15*weight_credit The grader selects the maximum-credit one-to-one component matching. component_score is the sum of matched pair credits divided by the larger of the predicted and true component counts. Missing and extra components are therefore penalized. count_score = max(0, 1 - abs(pred_count - true_count) / 2) For the three treatment tokens, the grader finds a maximum one-to-one matching. A matched token pair receives max(0, 1 - abs(pred-true)/3). Precision and recall use this soft credit, and plan_score is their F1. Artifact events are matched the same way with tolerance 2 instead of 3. artifact_score is the resulting soft F1. The row score is: independent = 0.64*component_score 0.10*count_score 0.18*plan_score 0.08*artifact_score core = independent * (0.78 + 0.22*min(component_score, plan_score)) calibration = max(0, 1 - abs(confidence - core)) row_score = 0.97core + 0.03calibration The final score is the arithmetic mean of row_score over all hidden test episodes. An ExtraTrees model using the full sequence plus interpolated vector and gradient features scores 0.488678, compared with 0.419614 using only protocol metadata and 0.378386 for a training-mean prior. The perfect oracle scores 1.0. These are local measurements, not platform-agent results, and do not establish that GPU models necessarily outperform classical methods. The supplied sample is a format example, not the strongest non-neural baseline. Dataset The prepared dataset contains 10,000 labelled training episodes and 2,500 hidden test episodes.
